module_title: IELTS Speaking Part 2: The Long Turn
lesson_title: Describe a Skill You Learned as an Adult
passage_or_prompt:
In Part 2 you get a task card, one minute to prepare (with paper and pencil), and then you speak for 1-2 minutes without interruption.

TASK CARD
Describe a skill you learned as an adult.
You should say:
- what the skill is
- when and how you learned it
- what difficulties you had
and explain how this skill has helped you.

ONE-MINUTE PLAN: write 3-4 key words for each bullet, NOT full sentences.
Example notes: driving / 25, after moving / instructor, 20 lessons / reverse parking, nervous / independence, job.

TIP: Use past tenses for the story, then switch to the present perfect to explain the result ('It has given me...').

questions.prompt: What should you do in the one-minute preparation time?
options: A. Write a full script to read out
B. Write key words for each bullet point
questions.correct_answer: B. Write key words for each bullet point
questions.explanation: There isn't time for a full script, and reading aloud sounds unnatural. Key words keep you on track and help you cover every bullet.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: 'Since then, it ______ (make) my life much easier.'
questions.explanation: 'Since then' connects a past event to the present, so the present perfect ('has made') is needed. Accurate tense control across a story is a key Band 6.5-7 feature.

questions.prompt: You finish speaking after 50 seconds. What is the best thing to do?
options: B. Add more detail about a bullet point, such as a specific difficulty or feeling
C. Start talking about a different topic
D. Repeat what you already said
questions.correct_answer: B. Add more detail about a bullet point, such as a specific difficulty or feeling
questions.explanation: Aim to speak until the examiner stops you. Expanding on a bullet point -- especially with feelings, a short story or a comparison -- is the most natural way to extend your answer.

band_9_sample:
I'd like to talk about learning to drive, which I didn't actually do until I was twenty-five.

I grew up in a big city with excellent public transport, so I never really needed a car. But when I moved to a regional town for work, I quickly realised that without a licence I was stuck -- the buses only ran a few times a day. So I booked a course with a local instructor and took about twenty lessons over three months.

To be honest, it was harder than I expected. Most of my friends had learned as teenagers, and I felt a bit embarrassed being a beginner at my age. Reverse parking was my nightmare -- I must have practised it a hundred times in an empty car park before I could do it without hitting the kerb. And I was so nervous before my test that I barely slept the night before.

Luckily, I passed on my first attempt, and since then it has made my life so much easier. I can get to work without relying on anyone, I've been able to apply for jobs that require a licence, and I've explored parts of the country I would never have seen otherwise. More than anything, though, it taught me that it's never too late to learn something new -- you just have to accept feeling a bit awkward at the start.
